en: The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent and Attainment of Buddhahood, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Śāriputra of Great Wisdom was able to follow the Buddha in turning the wheel of the Dharma; he was a great general of the Buddha-dharma.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

As it has been taught in the sūtras of the past and present, Maitreya is about to become a Buddha. I wish to hear extensively of Maitreya’s merits, his supernormal powers, and the adornments of his land."
“By what kind of giving, what kind of precepts, and what kind of wisdom do sentient beings come to see Maitreya?
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“I shall now explain this to you in detail; you should listen with a single-minded focus.”
Śāriputra! The waters of the four great oceans gradually decrease by three thousand yojanas;
at that time, the land of Jambudvīpa will be ten thousand yojanas long and eight thousand yojanas wide, as level as a mirror, with fragrant flowers and soft grasses covering its surface everywhere.
The various trees were lush with flowers and fruit, each reaching a height of thirty *li*;
the cities and towns stood close together, such that a rooster could fly from one to the next.
The lifespan of the people was eighty-four thousand years; they were endowed with wisdom, majesty, physical beauty, and strength, living in peace, security, and happiness.
There are only three ailments: first, the need for excretion; second, the need for food and drink; and third, old age. Women do not marry until they are five hundred years of age.

"At that time, there was a great city named Kukkutavati, twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in breadth. It was magnificent and exquisite, adorned and pure, and filled with people of merit; because of these meritorious people, it was prosperous, joyful, and peaceful."
The city was composed of the seven treasures; its upper stories, pavilions, doors, windows, and balconies were all made of various jewels, and nets of pearls covered them from above.
The streets, lanes, and thoroughfares were twelve li wide, swept clean, and sprinkled with water.
There is a powerful dragon king named Talaśikhin; his pool is near the city, and the dragon king’s palace is within this pool.
Constantly at midnight, he sends down a fine rain to settle the dust.
The ground was moist and lustrous, as if smeared with oil; as people traveled back and forth, no dust arose.
This was due to the merit and virtue of the people of that age; throughout the streets and alleys, there were pillars of bright pearls, each ten *li* in height.
Its radiance was so brilliant that there was no difference between day and night; the light of lamps and candles was no longer of any use.
The cities, houses, and all the streets and alleys—even down to the smallest clod of earth—were entirely covered with golden sand, and in every place there were heaps of gold and silver.
There is a great yakṣa deity named Bhadrapālaśaka—translated into the language of Qin as "Good Instruction"—who constantly protects this city and keeps it swept clean;
if there is any excrement or impurity, the earth cracks open to receive it, and having received it, it closes back up again.
When people’s lives were about to end, they would naturally proceed to the burial grounds to die.
At that time, the world was peaceful and secure, free from the calamities of enemies or bandits and robbery;
in the cities, towns, and villages, no one had to close their gates, nor did there exist the afflictions of decay, nor the hardships of water, fire, weapons, famine, or poison.
People there are always compassionate in heart, respectful and harmonious, having subdued their sense faculties and speaking with humility. "Śāriputra!
I shall now describe for you, in brief, the matters concerning the wealth, joy, cities, and districts of that land."

Within those various groves and gardens, and amidst the ponds and springs, there naturally appeared water endowed with the eight qualities, and lotuses of various colors—blue, red, crimson, and white—completely covering their surfaces.

On the four sides of that pond were stairways made of the four precious substances. Various birds gathered there in harmony: geese, ducks, mandarin ducks, peacocks, kingfishers, parrots, śāris, kuṇālas, jīvañjīvakas, and other such birds of exquisite song; these always dwelt therein, along with countless other species of wondrously singing birds.
Fruit trees and fragrant trees filled the land.

At that time, Jambudvīpa was constantly endowed with exquisite perfumes, like the Fragrant Mountain (Gandhamādana). Its flowing waters were beautiful, their taste sweet and capable of removing ailments. Rain fell according to the seasons, and the crops flourished. Weeds did not grow, and from a single sowing there were seven harvests; little labor was required, yet the yield was great. The food was fragrant and delicious, and people’s physical strength was fully restored.
"At that time in that land, there was a wheel-turning monarch named Śaṅkha, who ruled over the four continents with his fourfold army, not by means of military force."
That king had a thousand sons, valiant and possessed of great strength, capable of defeating enemies.
The king possessed the seven treasures:
the golden wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the steward treasure, and the military commander treasure.
Furthermore, in that land there are towers made of the seven precious substances, rising to a height of a thousand *zhang*, with a thousand heads and a thousand wheels, and sixty *zhang* in width.
There are also four great treasuries; each great treasury is surrounded by four hundred million smaller treasuries:

the great *Ilerbata* treasury is in the kingdom of Gandhāra; the great *Panzhujiaka* treasury is in the kingdom of Mithilā; the great *Pingala* treasury is in the kingdom of Sūrata; and the great *Śaṅkha* treasury is in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
These four great treasuries are each one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with precious jewels, and each has four hundred million smaller treasuries attached to it;
there are four great dragon kings, each guarding one respectively.
These four great treasuries and various minor treasuries spontaneously emerged, shaped like lotus flowers; countless people all went together to behold them.

At that time, although the many jewels had no guardians, when the multitude saw them, their hearts felt no greed or attachment; they cast them upon the ground as if they were tiles, stones, grass, wood, or clods of earth.
Those of that time who saw it all conceived a sense of revulsion and thought:

"In the past, for the sake of this treasure, sentient beings harmed one another, plundered and robbed each other, practiced deception and falsehood, causing the conditions for the cycle of birth and death and their karmic offenses to increase ever further."

In the city of Ketumatī, nets of various jewels completely cover it above; adorned with precious bells, when stirred by a gentle breeze, their sound is harmonious and elegant, like the striking of bells and chimes.
“In that city there was a great Brahmin lord named Miao-fan (Subrahmanya);
the Brahmin woman was named Fan-mo-po-ti (Brahmāvatī). Maitreya took birth as their son;

his body was the color of purple gold and possessed the thirty-two marks. When sentient beings beheld him, they could never tire of looking. His physical strength was immeasurable and inconceivable; his radiance shone so brightly that it encountered no obstruction, such that the sun, moon, fire, and mani-jewels no longer appeared at all.”
His height was one thousand *zhī*, his chest spanned thirty *zhàng*, and his face measured twelve *zhàng* and four *chí*.

His body was complete and upright beyond compare; he was endowed with the primary and secondary marks of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), like a cast golden image. His physical eyes were pure and could see for ten *yojana*; his constant radiance shone in the four directions for a hundred *yojana*, such that the light of the sun, moon, fire, and mani-jewels no longer appeared, for there was only the Buddha’s light, subtle and supreme.

“Maitreya Bodhisattva, observing the five desires of the world, he saw that they bring about many afflictions; sentient beings are submerged and sinking within the great cycle of birth and death, which is truly pitiable.
Because he observes with such right mindfulness, he takes no pleasure in the household life.”
At that time, King Śaṅkha, together with his various ministers, took this precious terrace and offered it to Maitreya;
having accepted it, Maitreya gave it to the brahmins;
and having accepted it, the brahmins immediately demolished it and divided it among themselves.
Maitreya Bodhisattva, seeing that this wondrous terrace was impermanent even in an instant, realized that all phenomena are likewise subject to decay and extinction;

cultivating the perception of impermanence, he left the household life to study the Way and sat beneath the Dragon Flower Bodhi tree—a tree whose trunk, branches, and leaves rose fifty *li* high—and on the very day he left home, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the kings of the devas, nāgas, and yakṣas did not manifest their bodies, yet they rained down flowers and incense as an offering to the Buddha;
the trichiliocosm shook violently, and light issued from the Buddha’s body, illuminating immeasurable lands, so that all those who were ready to be delivered were able to see the Buddha.
At that time, the people each had this thought:

"Even if one were to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses for thousands of millions of billions of years, one cannot escape the suffering of the three evil realms; wives, children, and property cannot provide salvation. The world is impermanent, and life is difficult to preserve for long."
"We should now practice the holy life within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Having formed this thought, they left the household life to study the Way.
At that time, King Śaṅkha, likewise surrounded by eighty-four thousand ministers who paid him respectful homage, also left the household life to study the Way.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand brahmins, wise and of great intelligence, who likewise went forth together within the Buddha’s Dharma;
there was also a householder named Sudatta—this very Sudatta the Elder—who likewise went forth together with eighty-four thousand people;
and there were also the brothers Liśāda and Pūraṇa, who likewise went forth with eighty-four thousand people.

Furthermore, there were two chief ministers, one named Candana and the other named Sumana, whom the king held in great esteem; they also, together with eighty-four thousand people, went forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
King Śaṅkha’s precious daughter, named Śamīvatī—she is the present Viśākhā—also, together with eighty-four thousand court ladies, went forth into homelessness.
King Śaṅkha’s crown prince, named Devavarṇa—he is the present Devaśarman—also, together with eighty-four thousand people, went forth into homelessness.

The kinsman of Maitreya Buddha, a son of a brāhmaṇa named Sumati, who possessed keen faculties and wisdom, is now Uttara; he too, together with eighty-four thousand people, has gone forth from the household life within the Buddha-dharma.
Countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings such as these, seeing the suffering and affliction of the world, all went forth into homelessness within the Dharma of Maitreya Buddha.
At that time, Maitreya Buddha, seeing the great assembly, thought to himself:

"These people have not come to me for the sake of the joy of rebirth in heaven, nor for the sake of the pleasures of this present life; they have come solely for the sake of the causes and conditions for the eternal bliss of Nirvāṇa."

"All these people have planted various roots of goodness within the Buddha-dharma; Śākyamuni Buddha has sent them to entrust them to me. For this reason, they have all come to my place now, and I now receive them."
These people, having cultivated various merits by means of reciting, studying, analyzing, and definitively determining the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma Piṭakas, have come to my presence.
Some have come to my presence having practiced these meritorious deeds by giving clothing and food to others, maintaining the precepts, and cultivating wisdom;
others have come to my presence having practiced these meritorious deeds by making offerings of banners, canopies, flowers, and incense to the Buddha.
Some have come to my presence having practiced the merit of giving, observing the fasts, and cultivating a mind of loving-kindness;
others have come to my presence having cultivated this merit for the sake of suffering sentient beings, so as to enable them to attain happiness.
Some, by means of upholding the precepts and practicing patience, cultivate pure loving-kindness; through these merits, they come to my presence.
Others, by providing the Sangha with regular meals, or by establishing assemblies for fasting and preaching to offer food and sustenance, cultivate such merits and thus come to my presence.
Some come to my presence by means of upholding the precepts and extensive learning, practicing meditative concentration and untainted wisdom; through these merits, they come to me.
Others come to my presence by erecting stupas and making offerings to the relics; through these merits, they come to me.
“Excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!
You have skillfully taught and transformed hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings such as these, causing them to come to my place.
After Maitreya Buddha had thus praised Śākyamuni Buddha three times, he then preached the Dharma, saying:

“You sentient beings have been able to perform a difficult task; that amidst those people of the evil age—possessed of greed, anger, ignorance, delusion, and short lifespans—you are able to cultivate and maintain the precepts and perform various meritorious deeds is truly rare and marvelous.”
At that time, sentient beings did not recognize their parents;

śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas did not know the Way and its Dharma. They harmed one another, drawing near to the kalpa of weapons. Deeply attached to the five desires, they were envious, sycophantic, crooked, fawning, turbid, and deceitful. Lacking any heart of compassion, they killed and harmed one another, eating flesh and drinking blood.
That you are able to practice virtuous deeds therein is truly rare.
Excellent, Śākyamuni Buddha!
With a heart of great compassion, you are able to speak truthful words amidst suffering and afflicted sentient beings, showing me that you shall come in the future to deliver and liberate us.

A teacher such as this is extremely difficult to encounter; with a profound heart of compassion, he pities the sentient beings of this degenerate age, rescuing them from suffering and distress to bring them peace and security.
For your sake, Śākyamuni Buddha gave away his head, cut off his ears, nose, hands, feet, limbs, and body parts, and underwent all manner of suffering and affliction to benefit you.
“Maitreya Buddha will thus guide and comfort immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to rejoice, and only then will he preach the Dharma.
Persons of merit will fill that realm; they will receive it with reverence and faith, longing for the Great Teacher and each desiring to hear the Dharma. They will all think:

‘The five desires are impure, the root of all suffering; they can further eliminate sorrow, grief, and affliction, and one comes to know that both painful and pleasant phenomena are all impermanent.’”

Maitreya Buddha observed the great assembly gathered at that time; their minds were pure, disciplined, and supple. He preached the Four Noble Truths for them, and those who heard it simultaneously attained the path to Nirvana.
"At that time, Maitreya Buddha will be in the Flower Forest Garden (*Puṣpavana*). That garden is one hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, and the great assembly fills it.
At his first assembly for preaching the Dharma, nine billion six hundred million people will attain arhatship;
at his second great assembly for preaching the Dharma, nine billion four hundred million people will attain arhatship."
At the third great assembly for preaching the Dharma, ninety-two billion people attained arhatship.
Once Maitreya Buddha had set the wheel of Dharma in motion and delivered both devas and humans, he led his disciples into the city to beg for alms.
An immeasurable multitude of Śuddhāvāsa devas followed the Buddha with reverence and entered the city of Ketumatī.
As they entered the city, he manifested various supernormal powers and countless transformations.

Śakra-devānām-indra, together with the devas of the desire realm, and Brahmā-rāja, together with the devas of the form realm, performed hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues. They rained down celestial flowers and powdered sandalwood incense as offerings to the Buddha;
along the streets, lanes, and pathways, they erected various banners and canopies and burned many kinds of famous incense, the smoke of which rose like clouds.
When the World-Honored One entered the city, Mahābrahmā and Śakra-devendra joined their palms in reverent salutation and praised him with these verses:
“The Perfectly All-Knowing One, the Honored One among two-legged beings, Is without equal in the world of gods and men.
The World-Honored One of the Ten Powers is most rare and marvelous; He is the unsurpassed, supreme, and excellent field of merit.”
"Those who make offerings to him will be born in the heavens; we prostrate to the peerless one of great diligence.

At that time, when the devas, humans, rākṣasas, and others saw the Buddha subduing the powerful Māra, immeasurable beings numbering in the thousands of myriads of koṭis were filled with great joy. Joining their palms, they cried out:
"How truly rare! How marvelous!"
"How truly rare!
The Tathāgata’s supernormal powers and his fulfillment of merit are inconceivable.

At that time, the devas and humans scattered various multicolored lotuses and māndārava flowers before the Buddha, piling them up to his knees; meanwhile, in the sky, they performed hundreds of thousands of musical instruments and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
At that time, during the first watch and the last watch of the night, the Māra-king awakened the people and spoke these words:
"Since you have obtained this human body and encountered such a favorable time, you should not spend the entire night with sleep shrouding your minds.
Whether standing or sitting, you should always be diligent and energetic, maintaining right mindfulness, and clearly contemplate the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
"Do not be negligent, do not fail to practice the Buddha's teaching; if you give rise to evil karma, you will surely come to regret it later.
At that time, the men and women in the streets and alleys all imitated these words, saying:
"Do not be negligent, do not fail to practice the Buddha's teaching; if you give rise to evil karma, there will certainly be regret later."
You should diligently apply skillful means and strive with vigor to seek the Way; do not lose the benefit of the Dharma so that your life is lived in vain and your death is in vain.
Such a Great Master who uproots suffering and distress is exceedingly difficult to encounter; through firm and steadfast vigor, you shall attain the eternal bliss of Nirvana.

“At that time, all the disciples of Maitreya Buddha will be universally upright and handsome, fully endowed with dignified deportment. Weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death, they will be widely learned and deeply cultivated, guarding the treasury of the Dharma and practicing meditative concentration. They will attain liberation from all desires, like a bird emerging from its shell.”

At that time, Maitreya Buddha, wishing to go to where the Elder Mahākāśyapa was, immediately accompanied by the fourfold assembly, proceeded to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; from the summit of the mountain, he beheld Mahākāśyapa.
At that time, the great assembly of men and women were all struck with wonder.
Maitreya Buddha praised him, saying:
"The bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa is a great disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha; among the great assembly, Śākyamuni Buddha has always praised him as the foremost in dhūta practices."

Having attained mastery over dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, although this person possesses great supernormal powers, they harbor no sense of superiority; they are able to cause sentient beings to attain great joy, and they constantly take pity on those who are lowly, poor, and afflicted, rescuing them from suffering and distress to bring them peace and security.
Maitreya Buddha praised the skeletal remains of Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, O one of great divine virtue!
Mahākāśyapa, the great disciple of the Lion of the Śākyas, was able to cultivate his mind even in that evil age."

At that time, when the great assembly saw Mahākāśyapa being praised by Maitreya Buddha, hundreds of thousands of billions of people, because of this event, grew weary of the world and attained the Way.
These people, mindful of Śākyamuni Buddha, who in this evil age taught and transformed immeasurable sentient beings, enabling them to attain the six supernormal powers and become arhats.
At that time, the place where the Dharma was being preached was eighty yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas long;
among the multitude of people there, whether sitting or standing, near or far, each individual saw the Buddha before them alone, preaching the Dharma specifically for them.
“Maitreya Buddha will remain in the world for sixty thousand years, out of compassion for sentient beings, enabling them to attain the Dharma-eye;
after his parinirvāṇa, the Dharma will likewise remain in the world for sixty thousand years.”

"You all should apply yourselves with diligence, arouse a pure mind, and cultivate various wholesome deeds; then you will surely behold the body of Maitreya Buddha, the Lamp of Illumination for the World—of this there is no doubt."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra and the others received it with joy and upheld it.
The Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent to Rebirth and Attainment of Buddhahood.
